name: Baraïn
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 further works by the same author (or citing it for stress) agree.
catalog_citation: Lovestrand, Joseph. 2012. The Linguistic Structure of Baraïn (Chadic). MA thesis, Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics (Dallas). PDF:https://www.diu.edu/documents/theses/Lovestrand_Joseph-thesis.pdf
catalog_locator: Chapter 5 'Tone', opening paragraph, printed p.52 (p.69); abstract; section 5.5 'Intonation' p.67
catalog_quote: Baraïn, like all known Chadic languages, is tonal (Newman 2006:193; Frajzyngier & Shay 2012:246). Three levels of tone are contrastive in the lexicon. No grammatical tone has been discovered other than the phrase-final effects described as intonation below (section 5.5). There is just one example in the data of a minimal triplet contrasting all three levels of tone. (99) [átːá] 'arm' [ātːá] '(number of) times' [àtːá] 'stomach' ... There is no predictable relationship between tone and vowel length or tone and voicing (i.e., no consonant-tone interference).

new_statements.quote: 3.3 Tone. One final phonological trait, which distinguishes one dialect of Baraïn from another, is the levels of tone used. Jalkiya use three levels of phonemic tone.7 The wordlist for Jalking gives evidence of three levels of tone, at least phonetically. The Komiya wordlist, on the other hand, only shows evidence for two levels of tone. [fn. 7:] Tone was not transcribed for the short wordlist done for the Giliya. However, given the high level of lexical similarity between Jalkiya and Giliya, it is likely that Giliya also has three levels of tone. [p. 11:] A remarkable trait of the Jalking wordlist is that nearly every word contains at least one heavy syllable; only 14 of the 258 words do not have a heavy syllable. Of those 244 words with a heavy syllable, the first syllable of the word is heavy 232 times. It is not known if this pattern is due to a lexical restriction or if it arises from a synchronic phonological process.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: the PDF's metadata confirms) with extracted text dump. The quoted §3.3 Tone passage and footnote 7 are verbatim on p.11 (printed p.10); the 'A remarkable trait of the Jalking wordlist.. synchronic phonological process' passage is verbatim on p.12 (printed p.11); Table 11 on p.16 (printed p.15) gives Tone: Jalking 3 levels, Komi 2 levels, Giliya 3 levels, Jalkiya 3 levels. My own a full-text search for stress/accent the whole text for stress|accent|prominen|emphas|intensity|loud returns only 'cloud' (gloss in the wordlist): the paper never mentions stress or accent, so tone language, no stress statement is the right reading. Relation: the catalog record (verified against the source) is tonal…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's 'tonal' record (three contrastive levels, no stress rule stated, from Lovestrand 2012 MA thesis on Jalkiya): this earlier paper gives the same three-level tone picture for Jalkiya and adds the dialect comparison (Komiya two levels). It is silent on stress, which is compatible with the catalog's 'no word-stress or accent rule is stated'. The heavy-initial-syllable count for Jalking is a wordlist phonotactic observation about the eastern variety (saka1296), not a stress statement for bare1279.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every Baraïn dialect is described as tonal: Jalkiya has three phonemic tone levels, Jalking three levels at least phonetically, Komiya two levels, Giliya untranscribed but presumed three (fn. 7). The paper never mentions stress, accent or prominence (0 hits for stress/accent/prominen in the full text). The only prominence-adjacent remark is a phonotactic one about the Jalking wordlist: 232 of 258 words have a heavy first syllable, which the author explicitly leaves unexplained ('lexical restriction or.. synchronic phonological process') and does not call stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: Komiya shows only two tone levels versus three in the other dialects (Table 11); Giliya tone not transcribed. 14 of 258 Jalking words lack a heavy syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Lovestrand 2011 compares four Baraïn dialects: Jalkiya and Giliya (central, the lects described in the 2012 MA thesis, the 2018 DPhil and the 2022 book), Komiya (south/west, two tone levels, retains implosives) and Jalking (east; Glottolog splits it off as saka1296). The tone statements quoted cover all four; the heavy-initial-syllable passage concerns the Jalking wordlist only. The 2022 book, per its abstract, is on Barayin generally (Jalkiya-based per all prior work).

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the only grammar of Baraïn (Lovestrand 2012, 311 pp, dedicated tone chapter), which we hold; the deciding quotation is verbatim at the cited page (printed p.52 / p.69) and the section 5.5 intonation quote at p.67. The author's later works (2018 DPhil downloaded now from ORA; 2022 OUP book per Crossref chapter list) are morphosyntactic and restate that Barayin is tonal with low functional load, with no word-stress or accent claim anywhere. No independent phonology/prosody study of the language exists in Glottolog or the author's own bibliographies. Coding 'tonal, no stress rule stated, domain not stated by the source' stands; nothing to reclassify. tx

sources.quote: p.74: 'Although Barayin is a tonal language, the functional load of contrastive tone is relatively low. Minimal pairs are relatively infrequent. ... In several places in the pronominal system, the second-person and third-person plural forms are distinguished by tone.' p.52: 'Chadic languages are tonal. There are often two contrastive levels of tone, sometimes three.' No mention of word stress or accent anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: 'stress' only in an English focus-reading remark; 'prosody' only re SVC prosodic unity).
